Sovereignty of God
SOV-rin-tee of GOD
noun phrase (theology proper / divine attributes)
The divine attribute by which God exercises supreme, absolute, and universal rule over all His creation, governing all things according to the counsel of His own will. Grounded in the divine kingship and dominion (Psalm 103:19, his kingdom ruleth over all; Daniel 4:35; Ephesians 1:11, who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will). Central to Reformed theology.

📖 Biblical Definition

The divine attribute by which God exercises supreme, absolute, and universal rule over all His creation, governing all things according to the counsel of His own will. The sovereignty of God is the substantive heart of Reformed theology, the truth that God is King over all, working all things according to His eternal purpose. The biblical foundation: (1) God's universal kingship and dominion — The LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all (Psalm 103:19); he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou? (Daniel 4:35); (2) God works all things according to His will — who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will (Ephesians 1:11); The LORD hath made all things for himself (Proverbs 16:4); Our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased (Psalm 115:3); (3) God's sovereignty in creation (Genesis 1; all things made by His word), providence (Matthew 10:29-30, not a sparrow falls without the Father; Colossians 1:17, by Him all things consist), and salvation (Romans 9, the sovereignty of God in election and reprobation; Ephesians 1:4-11, election according to the good pleasure of His will); (4) God's sovereignty over the nations, kings, and history (Daniel 2:21, he removeth kings, and setteth up kings; Daniel 4:17, the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men; Proverbs 21:1, the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD); (5) God's sovereignty even over evil, which He ordains and overrules for His good purposes without being the author of sin (Genesis 50:20, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good; Acts 2:23, Christ delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God yet by wicked hands crucified; Acts 4:27-28). The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession III on God's eternal decree; V on providence) holds that God from all eternity did freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as neither to be the author of sin nor to do violence to the will of the creatures. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's sovereignty as the heart of Reformed theology, against the open-theist and process-theology denials (which limit God's sovereignty), the deistic conception (which removes God's active governance), and the man-centered theologies (which subordinate God's sovereignty to human autonomy). God is sovereign — supreme, absolute, and universal in His rule, working all things according to the counsel of His own will — and His sovereignty is the substantive ground of the believer's confidence, comfort, and worship: nothing is outside God's control, all things work together for good to them that love God (Romans 8:28), and the King who reigns over all is the believer's Father.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The divine attribute by which God exercises supreme, absolute, universal rule over all creation, governing all things according to the counsel of His will; Psalm 103:19 (his kingdom ruleth over all), Daniel 4:35, Ephesians 1:11 (who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will); the heart of Reformed theology; held over creation, providence, salvation, the nations, and even evil (without being the author of sin).

SOVEREIGNTY OF GOD, n. phr. (theology proper / divine attributes) God exercises supreme, absolute, universal rule over all creation, governing all things according to the counsel of His own will. The heart of Reformed theology. Foundation: Psalm 103:19 (his kingdom ruleth over all); Daniel 4:35 (none can stay his hand); Ephesians 1:11 (who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will); Psalm 115:3 (he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased). Over creation, providence (Matthew 10:29-30), salvation (Romans 9; Ephesians 1:4-11), the nations and kings (Daniel 2:21; Proverbs 21:1), and even evil (ordained and overruled for good without being the author of sin, Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). Westminster III, V. Held against open theism, process theology, deism, and man-centered theologies.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 103:19 — "The LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all."

Daniel 4:35 — "And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?"

Ephesians 1:11 — "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will."

Genesis 50:20 — "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The sovereignty of God is the heart of Reformed theology; held against open theism and process theology (limiting God's sovereignty), deism (removing active governance), and man-centered theologies (subordinating sovereignty to human autonomy); God works all things after the counsel of His will without being the author of sin.

expand to see more

The sovereignty of God is the substantive heart of Reformed theology, held against several errors. Open theism and process theology limit God's sovereignty, denying that God ordains and controls all things (open theism holds that God does not know or determine the free future actions of creatures; process theology makes God a developing participant in a process He does not control); this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God works all things after the counsel of His own will (Ephesians 1:11) and that none can stay His hand (Daniel 4:35). The deistic conception removes God's active governance, treating God as a distant creator who set the world in motion and does not actively rule it; this contradicts the biblical doctrine of God's active providence (Matthew 10:29-30; Colossians 1:17). The man-centered theologies (Arminianism in its various forms; the broader free-will theologies) subordinate God's sovereignty to human autonomy, making God's purposes contingent on the autonomous choices of the creature; this contradicts the biblical doctrine of God's sovereign election and His working of all things according to His will. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: God is sovereign — supreme, absolute, and universal in His rule, working all things according to the counsel of His own will; His sovereignty extends over creation, providence, salvation, the nations and kings, and even over evil (which He ordains and overrules for His good purposes without being the author of sin, the great mystery held in Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23). The Westminster Confession holds the substantive balance (III.1): God from all eternity did freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as neither to be the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures. The sovereignty of God is the substantive ground of the believer's confidence, comfort, and worship: nothing is outside God's control; all things work together for good to them that love God (Romans 8:28); the King who reigns supreme over all is the believer's loving Father, and His sovereign purposes cannot fail.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Psalm 103:19; Daniel 4:35; Ephesians 1:11; Psalm 115:3; Genesis 50:20; Westminster III, V; God's supreme, absolute, universal rule over all things according to the counsel of His will; the heart of Reformed theology.
